source.title: Epistemic diversity across language models mitigates knowledge collapse

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out perplexity as model and dataset size change during recursive self-training, and reports stronger collapse at larger model scale in low-diversity ecosystems. It argues that scaling behavior can invert in a low-data-quality regime.
record.gate_note: The study does not fit power laws or test prediction from small runs. Its relevant results are the stated perplexity effects of model and dataset scale during recursive self-training; the plotted values are not transcribed as numbers. Results on real-data incorporation, sampling temperature, and other sensitivity analyses are not recorded unless they bear directly on scaling behavior.
record.test_reason: In recursive fine-tuning on self-generated Wikitext2 data, the study compares two model sizes (125M vs 350M/355M) and two dataset sizes (0.8M vs 2.1M tokens) on held-out Wikitext2 perplexity. It reports that larger scale worsens perplexity in homogeneous ecosystems at later iterations, and argues that scaling laws invert in a low-data-quality regime. That is a training-regime result, so it bears on V5. It does not bear on V1: there is no pretraining and only two sizes are compared, so no power-law form can be shown.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that ecosystem diversity mitigates collapse, with the optimal diversity rising with iterations. Scaling up model and data size amplifies collapse in homogeneous ecosystems, and the authors hypothesise that scaling laws invert in a low effective-data-quality regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses small OPT and GPT2 models fine-tuned on recursively generated Wikitext2 outputs and evaluates perplexity across iterations. It does not fit the original scaling-law curves, conduct large-scale extrapolation, or optimize parameters and tokens under a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scale effects vary with self-training iteration, ecosystem diversity, model family, and dataset size.
record.problems: The scale experiments cover a limited range of relatively small model and dataset sizes and use recursive fine-tuning rather than ordinary pretraining. The relevant loss outcomes are described in prose and figures rather than reported as numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Results on real-data incorporation and sampling temperature, and additional sensitivity analyses, were left out because they do not test the scaling-law versions directly. See Sections 3.2 and Appendix J.

untested.parts: All of it. There is no pretraining, only fine-tuning on Wikitext2 and recursive outputs, with two sizes per axis and no power-law fit.
No shape comparison at fixed parameters.
The power-law form itself: only two model sizes and two dataset sizes, over less than one order of magnitude.
No fitted exponents or fitting choices.

missing.what: Increasing dataset size worsens performance for OPT-350m, except in the D=1 ecosystem. This is a reversal of data scaling.
For GPT2, solely increasing dataset size slightly decreases perplexity at D=1.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling results are a side variation using two sizes per axis in a fine-tuning and synthetic-data regime, so they show only the direction of the scale effect. The V1 and V7 links in the record are removed because no pretraining loss and no fitted law are involved.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fit power laws, test several orders of magnitude, vary compute, or test the claim specifically for ordinary held-out pretraining loss with other factors not bottlenecking.
No small-run fits or predictions for much larger runs.
Does not find a loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation for fixed compute.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Uses language models and recursive fine-tuning, but does not test whether power-law forms hold in these or other training regimes.
Does not test downstream task performance.
Does not compare fitted exponents, parameter-counting or fitting methods, or compute-optimal allocations. The evidence concerns scale-dependent loss behavior in recursive self-training.

rows.subject: OPT-350M
rows.operation_detail: Compared model-size scaling with OPT-125m at fixed dataset size during recursive self-training.
rows.measure: Mean perplexity on the original Wikitext2 test set
rows.baseline: OPT-125m (125M parameters), same dataset size and diversity setting
rows.value: Larger models show stronger perplexity increases in later iterations, indicating stronger collapse.
rows.uncertainty: Combined standard deviation across models and data points shown as shaded regions in Figure 4.
rows.note: The stated scale effect is for low-diversity recursive self-training, not ordinary pretraining.
rows.check: Not pretraining loss, so drop V1. No exponents are fitted, so drop V7. Figure 4(c) shows D=1; the D≤2 statement comes from the Section 3.1 text. Only two model sizes, so this shows direction only.
